newsitem.title: UK: Clarke faces showdown with Britain's right-wing.
newsitem.headline: Clarke faces showdown with Britain's right-wing.

text.p: Spare a thought for Britain's finance minister, Kenneth Clarke.

Since taking over the post of chancellor of the exchequer in 1993, he has presided over his country's soundest economic upturn for three decades and pushed the cost of home loans -- a subject dear to many Britons -- to the lowest for a generation.
Yet some colleagues on the right of the ruling Conservative party are baying for his blood.
His weakness, colleagues and media commentators agree, is that most rare political proclivity -- honesty.
"The trouble with Ken is that he is too honest and speaks his mind," one cabinet minister remarked last week.

Fresh from provoking a huge row by declaring that Britain would be "pathetic" if it dithered over joining a planned European Union single currency, Clarke said on Sunday voters would not respond to large, politically inspired tax cuts.

For the Conservative party's growing band of Eurosceptics, who are becoming increasingly influential as Britain grapples with moves towards tighter EU bonds, Clarke is not just out of order but should be sacked if he does not fall into line.

That would give the Conservatives, in power since 1979 and facing a general election within the next eight months, a chance to rule out joining a single European currency and cut taxes aggressively. That could put "clear blue water" between them and the opposition Labour party's brand of social democracy.

There are precedents. The Conservative party, a ruthless election-winning machine, dumped long-serving Margaret Thatcher as its leader in November 1990 and won a general election under her replacement, John Major, in April 1992.
But getting rid of Clarke and adopting a Thatcherite right-wing agenda would be tricky to execute and could easily backfire with financial markets and the electorate.

Clarke's pro-Europe views still represent an influential constituency in the Conservative party that includes Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine, and any move to ditch the chancellor could provoke more infighting, not less.

"The fact is a lot of Conservative members of parliament agree with Clarke and the cabinet has agreed a wait-and-see attitude on joining a single currency and that will remain," one party official said.
Any attempt to oust Clarke could also send shudders through domestic financial markets on fears the government might be set to "cut and run" in order to win an election due by May 1997.
Economists recall sterling's six-pfennig fall against the mark when the chancellor of the day, Nigel Lawson, quit in 1989.
The government has spent the past four years rebuilding its reputation for economic competence following sterling's stunning exit from the EU's currency grid in September 1992.

"If Clarke was forced out, British financial markets would fall sharply and interest rates could be forced higher," said Martin Weale, director of the National Institute for Economic and Social Research and a leading government adviser.

Britain's financial community, fed a diet of high inflation and double-digit interest rates in the 1970s and 1980s, has warmed to Clarke's brand of low inflation and sustainable growth, and his pro-European agenda.
Interest rates are just 5.75 percent though the Bank of England would like them higher, and the core rate of annual inflation is 2.8 percent and moving to a target of 2.5 percent.

That should add up to a golden economic scenario, but voters remain disgruntled and the much-vaunted "feel-good" factor has been slow to return, leaving the Conservatives as much as 30 percent adrift of the revamped Labour party in opinion polls.

Conservative sources say Clarke will be forced by Major to stick much more to the time-honoured convention of collective cabinet responsibility -- that all minister sing the same tune irrespective of their personal beliefs.
But Clarke, born into a working-class family with a father who was a coalmine electrician, may find it hard to pull his punches when confronted by the tax-cutting right of the party.

Indeed, Clarke has repeatedly said voters will not be bribed by big tax cuts and they must be consistent with the government aim to bring public borrowing -- which ballooned during the 1990-92 recession -- back into balance over the medium-term.

The smart money is on Clarke to survive his current political travails, but the real blood will be spilt if the Conservatives lost the election. Then Clarke, renowned as a bruiser, will a fight on his hands with the Eurosceptics.
